chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, who said: Isma'il ibn 'Umar narrated to me

that he had some dirhams owed to him by a man. The man offered to sell him food for those dirhams, payable after a specified term. Isma'il asked those who inquired about it, and he said, 'There is no harm in that.' Then Isma'il returned to him and asked him about it, saying, 'I had sent so-and-so to ask you about it, and you said there is no harm.' He said, 'What do the people at our place say about it?' I said, 'They say it is invalid (fasid).' He said, 'Do not do it, for I was mistaken.'
ai.seo_question: Is selling food for a debt with deferred payment valid or invalid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the scholarly principle of *takhfif* (leniency) versus *tashdid* (strictness) in early Shia jurisprudence, where a jurist's initial personal opinion (*ra'y*) is corrected upon consulting the consensus of the scholarly community. It highlights the concept of *wahm* (misconception or error) in legal reasoning, demonstrating that a jurit's ruling is not infallible and must align with the established views of the *ahl al-bayt*'s followers. This specific case of *bay' al-madmun* (selling a guaranteed debt) serves as a foundational example for understanding the evolution of transactional validity in the *Tahdhib*.
